system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2152-05-24 04:30:00 to 2152-05-25 11:07:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex medical history including morbid obesity, polymyositis, interstitial lung disease, diastolic heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, and recurrent venous thromboembolism was admitted for worsening dyspnea and right shin pain. She reported recent non-adherence to her diuretic and diabetes medications due to work demands. Evaluation revealed acute on chronic diastolic heart failure exacerbated by fluid retention, with no evidence of pulmonary embolism on CT. She was treated with IV furosemide and transitioned back to oral torsemide. The right shin lesion was evaluated by ultrasound, showing inflammatory changes consistent with cellulitis but no abscess; she was started on oral doxycycline and cephalexin. Her INR was subtherapeutic, so warfarin was increased to 6.5 mg daily. Urine and blood cultures showed no infection. She improved clinically, was discharged home, and instructed to follow up with her heart clinic and primary care provider for medication management and monitoring.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic (congestive) heart failure
Hypertensive heart disease with heart failure
Body mass index [BMI] 70 or greater, adult
Morbid (severe) obesity due to excess calories

storyline_prompt_block:
Discharge note 1 (2152-05-25 00:00:00): Name:  ___                Unit No:   ___
 
Admission Date:  ___              Discharge Date:   ___
 
Date of Birth:  ___             Sex:   F
 
Service: OBSTETRICS/GYNECOLOGY
 
Allergies: 
Miralax / Hydrochlorothiazide / Codeine / Benadryl / heparin / 
lisinopril
 
Attending: ___
 
Chief Complaint:
Abnormal pap smear, cervical dysplasia
 
Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
LEEP

 
Physical Exam:
Discharge physical exam
Vitals: VSS
Gen: NAD, A&O x 3
CV: RRR
Resp: no acute respiratory distress
Abd: soft, appropriately tender, no rebound/guarding
Ext: no TTP
 
Pertinent Results:
___ 07:21AM BLOOD ___ PTT-62.5* ___
 
Brief Hospital Course:
On ___, Ms. ___ was admitted to the gynecology service 
after undergoing a LEEP and endocervical curettage. Please see 
the operative report for full details. She was admitted for 
observation overnight given her multiple medical comorbidities.

*) Post-operative: Her post-operative course was uncomplicated. 
Immediately post-op, her pain was controlled with PO 
acetaminophen prn. Her diet was advanced without difficulty, and 
she denied any nausea/vomiting. She was able to void 
spontaneously on post-operative day #0. 

*) DVT/PE: Pt was continued on prophylactic lovenox 60mg BID 
while hospitalized. She also had pneumoboots bilaterally for 
mechanical prophylaxis. She was restarted on her home dose of 
Coumadin on post-operative day #1.

*) Diastolic congestive heart failure, HTN: Pt was continued on 
her home dose of torsemide, metoprolol, and losartan.

*) Interstitial lung disease, obstructive sleep apnea, asthma: 
Pt was continued on her home medications, used her CPAP/Bipap, 
and was monitored on telemetry. She did not have any evidence of 
respiratory distress and had oxygen saturations in the high ___ 
on room air prior to discharge.

*) T2DM: Pt was maintained on an insulin sliding scale on 
post-operative day #0. Her fingersticks blood glucose 
measurements ranged from 177-201.

By post-operative day #1, she was tolerating a regular diet, 
voiding spontaneously, ambulating independently, and pain was 
controlled with oral medications. She was then discharged home 
in stable condition with outpatient follow-up scheduled.
 
Discharge Medications:
1.  FLUoxetine 10 mg PO DAILY  
2.  GlipiZIDE XL 2.5 mg PO DAILY  
3.  liraglutide 1.8 mg subcutaneous DAILY  
4.  Losartan Potassium 25 mg PO DAILY  
5.  Metoprolol Succinate XL 100 mg PO DAILY  
6.  Torsemide 10 mg PO DAILY  
7.  Warfarin 6 mg PO DAILY Duration: 1 Dose  

 
Discharge Disposition:
Home
 
Discharge Diagnosis:
Cervical dysplasia

 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Out of Bed with assistance to chair or 
wheelchair.

 
Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

You were admitted to the gynecology service after your 
procedure. You have recovered well and the team believes you are 
ready to be discharged home. Please call Dr. ___ 
office with any questions or concerns. Please follow the 
instructions below.

General instructions:
* Take your medications as prescribed.
* Do not take more than 4000mg acetaminophen (APAP) in 24 hrs.
* Nothing in the vagina (no tampons, no douching, no sex) for 2 
weeks.
* You may eat a regular diet.
* You may walk up and down stairs.

Call your doctor for:
* fever > 100.4F
* severe abdominal pain
* difficulty urinating
* vaginal bleeding requiring >1 pad/hr
* abnormal vaginal discharge
* redness or drainage from incision
* nausea/vomiting where you are unable to keep down fluids/food 
or your medication

To reach medical records to get the records from this 
hospitalization sent to your doctor at home, call ___.
 
Followup Instructions:
___

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___? I'm Dr. ___ from the gynecology team. You just had a LEEP procedure for cervical dysplasia. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m a bit groggy, but okay. My lower belly is sore, nothing too bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The procedure went well. You’ll stay overnight for observation because of your other health conditions. We want to make sure everything stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was a little nervous about that. My heart and lungs have been tricky lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we reviewed your history. You have heart failure, lung disease, sleep apnea, and diabetes. That’s why we’re monitoring you closely. But so far, your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I take a lot of meds—warfarin, torsemide, insulin, and others. Should I take them today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We continued your torsemide, metoprolol, and losartan for your heart. You’ll get insulin based on fingerstick checks. And we’re giving Lovenox for blood clot prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped warfarin before the procedure. When do I restart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart your Coumadin tomorrow morning, once we’re sure there’s no bleeding risk. You’ll get 6 mg, same as your home dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. And my CPAP—I brought it. Should I use it tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please use your CPAP. We’ll monitor your oxygen levels. You’re on room air now and saturating well in the high 90s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had asthma flare-ups before if I don’t use it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep you on telemetry to watch your heart rhythm too. You had some tachycardia earlier, but it’s improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get anxious sometimes, especially in hospitals. That might make my heart race.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted your history of anxiety and depression. We’ll keep an eye on that. You’re on fluoxetine—still taking that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily. It helps. I just need to feel safe and informed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll keep you updated. For now, you can have sips of water. We’ll advance your diet as you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not nauseated. Can I try some juice later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once you keep water down, we’ll move to clear liquids, then a light meal. We want you eating normally before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update—your blood test this morning showed a PTT of 62.5, which is slightly elevated but expected with Lovenox. No concern for bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that related to my clotting? I’ve had blood clots before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have a history of venous thrombosis, so we’re being extra careful. Lovenox helps prevent clots, especially after surgery and with your immobility risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pneumatic boots? They’re a bit tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re squeezing your legs to keep blood moving. That’s another layer of protection. You’ll wear them until you’re up and walking well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You passed urine on your own, which is great. No nausea, and you’re alert. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s about a 3 out of 10. Acetaminophen helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll keep it as needed. Your blood sugars have been between 177 and 201. We’re using a sliding scale insulin to keep them in check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s higher than I like. I’m on glipizide and liraglutide at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart those when you’re fully on a regular diet. For now, insulin gives us more control. You’re not on any diabetes meds by mouth yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had lunch and kept it down. That’s a good sign. You’re also walking to the bathroom on your own?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with a little help at first, but now I’m steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That means you’re recovering well. We’ll plan to discharge you tomorrow morning if all stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I expect after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to avoid anything in the vagina—no tampons, douching, or sex—for two weeks. That helps prevent infection and lets the area heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—call if you have fever over 100.4, severe pain, heavy bleeding—more than one pad per hour—or difficulty urinating. Also, watch for redness or discharge from the incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds? When do I go back to my full list?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll restart all your home medications tomorrow, including warfarin 6 mg, glipizide, liraglutide, and the others. We’ll give you a list to take home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable, you’re walking well, and your pain is controlled. We’ve restarted your warfarin. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Follow up with your gynecologist in 2–3 weeks. Keep managing your heart, lungs, and diabetes as directed. And call if anything worries you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. You did great. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and get some rest at home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex medical history including chronic diastolic heart failure, interstitial lung disease, obstructive sleep apnea, asthma, type 2 diabetes, morbid obesity, and a history of venous thromboembolism was admitted for observation after undergoing a LEEP procedure for cervical dysplasia. She was monitored closely due to her comorbidities but had an uncomplicated post-operative course. Pain was controlled with acetaminophen, she advanced to a regular diet, voided spontaneously, and ambulated independently. She remained on home medications for heart and lung conditions, used CPAP, and was managed with insulin for glucose control. Prophylactic Lovenox and pneumatic boots were used for clot prevention, and warfarin was restarted before discharge. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to avoid vaginal activity for two weeks and to follow up with her gynecologist.
